title: She Was Handed Number 47. Nobody Ever Called It.
description:
On the morning of 6 September 1991 a sixty-five-year-old widow in Puerto Rico woke feeling, in her son's words, real bad: chills, cold sweat, dizziness, chest pains. She asked him to drive her to the emergency room where she had been treated before. She was inside no later than one o'clock.

A hospital employee gave Carmen Gonzalez a number, forty-seven, told her to bide her time, and checked her medical insurance card. After about an hour her son called his sister to relieve him, and as he left, at roughly a quarter past two, he heard an attendant call patient number twenty-four. She waited another forty-five to seventy-five minutes. No physician saw her. No vital signs were taken, and when the case was tried the hospital could not produce any records of the visit at all.

Weary of waiting, she and her daughter drove to the clinic her insurance plan designated for routine care, arriving between three and half past three. Her blood pressure was 90 over 60. The doctor started intravenous fluids, gave her something for the vomiting, and had to resuscitate her soon after she arrived. No ambulance could be obtained. At around half past four, as preparations were being made to move her by van, she died, and her death was attributed to hypovolemic shock. This film does not say the wait killed her, because the opinion does not: the damages that survived appeal were for what she went through while waiting, and for what her family lost.

A jury found that the hospital had failed to give her an appropriate screening and returned 700,000 dollars: 200,000 on the decedent's account, payable to the heirs, and 500,000 for the survivors, 100,000 each to three children and 50,000 each to four grandchildren. The trial judge refused to disturb any of it. On 31 October 1995 the First Circuit affirmed and did not reduce the award by a dollar.

The statute is EMTALA, and this was the First Circuit's first interpretation of it. A hospital satisfies the duty to screen, the court held, if it provides an examination reasonably calculated to identify critical medical conditions and provides that level of screening uniformly to all those who present substantially similar complaints. The essence of the requirement is that there be some screening procedure, and that it be administered even-handedly. Measured against the hospital's own written rules, which required staff to take every patient's vital signs promptly, make a written record of every visit, treat chest pain as critical and refer critical cases to an in-house physician immediately, the delay here was so egregious and lacking in justification as to amount to an effective denial of a screening examination. Motive was held to be no part of it: the duty runs to all patients who come to a hospital's emergency department, regardless of insurance status or ability to pay. EMTALA, the court wrote, should be read to proscribe both actual and constructive dumping of patients. Nobody in that building ever refused her anything.

What the court did not decide matters as much. It did not decide whether mere negligence in failing to expedite a screening would violate the statute. It did not review the jury's separate finding that she had been improperly transferred, because the screening finding alone sustained the verdict. It did not decide whether relatives can recover under EMTALA for their own anguish; the hospital raised that argument only after the verdict and it was held waived, pure and simple. And the statute promises less than its reputation: a screening, and stabilisation if an emergency condition is found, not treatment. An emergency room, the court said in the middle of its own holding, cannot serve everyone simultaneously.

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic; no real-person likeness is shown, and nothing about her death is dramatised.
Correa v. Hospital San Francisco, 69 F.3d 1184 (1st Cir. 1995).
